title: Triggers, Cravings, and Safer Choices
description: Helps parents identify internal and external substance-use triggers, notice early body warning signs, and practise immediate safer choices that protect children and recovery.

sections.title: Foundations & Baseline Understanding: Triggers, Cravings, and Safer Choices

content.title: Foundations & Baseline Understanding: Triggers, Cravings, and Safer Choices
content.overview: This section provides a trauma-informed, practical guide to understanding the core purpose of triggers, cravings, and safer choices and how it shapes physical, emotional, and relational safety in daily family life. Designed for parents building a practical trigger map and craving response plan (SS-CRS-AOD-002), it focuses on realistic, repeatable steps that strengthen safety, predictability, and connection.
content.psychoeducation: Why does triggers, cravings, and safer choices matter in section 1? Children and families thrive on predictability, nervous-system safety, and attuned repair. When triggers, cravings, and safer choices is practised consistently, stress responses decrease and relational trust grows. By focusing on understanding the core purpose of triggers, cravings, and safer choices and how it shapes physical, emotional, and relational safety in daily family life, caregivers and practitioners create a calmer, safer environment where children can regulate and develop confidence.
learning_goals: Define what triggers, cravings, and safer choices means in your own words before and after learning.
Recognise how triggers, cravings, and safer choices supports child safety, emotional wellbeing, and nervous-system regulation.
Practise simple, non-defensive scripts and responses for triggers, cravings, and safer choices during everyday moments.
Identify early warning signs, barriers, and support pathways related to triggers, cravings, and safer choices.
step_by_step: Pause & Ground: Notice your own breathing, body tension, and tone before addressing triggers, cravings, and safer choices.
Observe Factually: Notice what is happening in the moment around triggers, cravings, and safer choices without blame or judgement.
Connect & Validate: Acknowledge feelings and safety needs clearly and calmly.
Respond Simply: Choose one clear, age-appropriate action or boundary for triggers, cravings, and safer choices.
Reflect & Repair: Review what worked, repair any rupture honestly, and record your next small step.
parent_scripts: "I can see this moment feels big right now. Let's slow down and take one step together with triggers, cravings, and safer choices."
"Everyone is safe here. We can talk about what happened and work out the next step calmly."
"I noticed I was getting stressed. I'm taking a breath so I can listen properly."
"We don't have to get everything perfect today — we are practising triggers, cravings, and safer choices one routine at a time."
practical_examples: Everyday Routine: Applying triggers, cravings, and safer choices during a busy morning or bedtime transition by slowing down, offering two calm choices, and keeping tone steady.
Moment of Stress: When tension rises around triggers, cravings, and safer choices, pausing for 10 seconds before speaking, validating feelings, and focusing on safety first.
Follow-Through & Review: Recording a factual note after practising triggers, cravings, and safer choices to notice what helped the child settle and what support would help next time.
reflection_questions: What does triggers, cravings, and safer choices mean to me in my own words right now?
When is triggers, cravings, and safer choices easiest to practise, and what triggers make it hardest?
How does my child or family respond when I stay calm and predictable around triggers, cravings, and safer choices?
What is one specific, realistic action I will try this week to strengthen triggers, cravings, and safer choices?
practice_ideas: Complete the unassisted starting definition for triggers, cravings, and safer choices, then compare it with your end reflection.
Choose one daily routine this week to practise a calm, 2-sentence script for triggers, cravings, and safer choices.
Identify one trusted person, support service, or caseworker check-in to share your progress on triggers, cravings, and safer choices.
Write a brief, factual reflection note describing one moment you practised triggers, cravings, and safer choices and how your child responded.
content.closing_message: Progress in triggers, cravings, and safer choices comes from small, consistent moments of safety, honesty, and repair — not perfection. Every time you pause, stay regulated, and choose a safer response, you build lasting trust.

content_variants.toddlers: For babies & toddlers (0–4): Focus on gentle tone, physical comfort, predictable routines, and simple 3-to-5 word reassurance while practising triggers, cravings, and safer choices.
content_variants.school_age: For school-age children (5–11): Use clear explanations, visual routines, curiosity about their feelings, and collaborative problem-solving around triggers, cravings, and safer choices.
content_variants.teens: For adolescents (12–18): Respect autonomy, listen without lecturing, agree on clear safety boundaries, and involve teens in decisions about triggers, cravings, and safer choices.
content_variants.fatherhood: For fathers & male caregivers: Model calm accountability, steady emotional presence, and non-frightening leadership when practising triggers, cravings, and safer choices.

red_flags: Immediate physical danger, threats, intimidation, or coercive control observed during triggers, cravings, and safer choices.
A child shows fear, freezing, dissociation, or disclosure of harm related to triggers, cravings, and safer choices.
An adult is unable to regulate or maintain safe supervision while attempting triggers, cravings, and safer choices.
Signs of acute mental health crisis or substance intoxication affecting child safety.
when_to_escalate: Pause learning immediately if anyone is in danger and use verified emergency or crisis supports.
Follow jurisdiction-specific child protection and mandatory reporting obligations when harm is disclosed or suspected.
Engage a qualified supervisor, specialist DFV practitioner, or clinician when risk exceeds self-directed learning.

trauma_informed.clinical: Nervous-system lens for triggers, cravings, and safer choices: Recognises fight, flight, freeze, and fawn survival responses, window of tolerance, and the need for co-regulation before cognitive problem-solving.
trauma_informed.relational: Attachment lens for triggers, cravings, and safer choices: Prioritises connection before correction, attunement to cues, shame-free accountability, and timely repair after ruptures.
trauma_informed.justice: Fairness & cultural lens for triggers, cravings, and safer choices: Respects cultural strengths, kinship networks, neurodiversity, disability access, and structural barriers without equating poverty with neglect.
trauma_informed.fatherhood: Accountable fatherhood lens for triggers, cravings, and safer choices: Replaces control or withdrawal with steady, reliable care, honest repair, and child-centred safety.

sections.simplified_parent_version:
What triggers, cravings, and safer choices means:
Triggers, Cravings, and Safer Choices is about keeping daily life safe, calm, and predictable so your child feels supported and understood.

How to practise it:
1. Pause and take one slow breath first.
2. Notice what your child needs right now.
3. Use a calm voice and one clear step.
4. Repair kindly if things go off track.
